data.title: Middle East Eye: Eisenkot calls Netanyahu's unity government call 'yet another spin move'
data.author: Hilal Saki
data.summary:
Eisenkot calls Netanyahu's unity government call 'yet another spin move'
Israeli opposition leader and prime ministerial hopeful Gadi Eisenkot has accused Benjamin Netanyahu of resorting to political tricks to delay the formation of a new government, saying his latest call for negotiations was "yet another spin move".
In a post on X, Eisenkot said Netanyahu knew that a meeting between the negotiating teams of Likud and Yesh Atid had already been scheduled for Monday.
"This is the latest bluff: Netanyahu calls for negotiations after they have already been scheduled, claims he wants unity, but disgraces a state ceremony in the Knesset and divides and incites as if there were no tomorrow," Eisenkot wrote.
The remarks come after an inconclusive election left the Knesset without a clear governing majority, with rival political camps seeking to assemble the numbers needed to form the next government.
Eisenkot said Netanyahu knew he had lost the election and that there was "an overwhelming majority against him among the citizens of Israel and in the Knesset".
He accused the outgoing prime minister of mounting "a delaying action" to make it difficult to form a new government and prevent the replacement of the Knesset speaker.
Eisenkot reiterated that the conditions for joining an emergency government under his leadership included acceptance of the principles he had outlined and "a break with the extremists".

data.title: Middle East Eye: Trump may not attack Iran as long as it doesn't provoke US, report says
data.author: Hilal Saki
data.summary:
Trump may not attack Iran as long as it doesn't provoke US, report says
President Donald Trump has told senior advisers in recent days that he may hold off on attacking Iran if the US faces no new provocations from Tehran or the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen, according to three people familiar with the matter.
Trump has alternated between threats of escalating the war with new strikes and winding down hostilities, and current and former officials say he does not appear to have made up his mind about how to resolve the unpopular conflict, which he launched in February with Israel.
But in meetings with his national security advisers and after a series of intelligence briefings, Trump said he was considering holding off on strikes, said the people, who, like others interviewed for this story, spoke on condition of anonymity.
He has also indicated sympathy for allies in the region who have asked him not to return to a full-fledged war.
"I could end it immediately, but at the request of the nations that I am looking to protect, we are doing it a little bit longer way, a bit more civilly," Trump told sports broadcaster Stephen A. Smith on Thursday.
Trump's private comments build on public remarks playing down the likelihood of major warfare resuming.
CALLS WITH SAUDI ARABIA AND TURKEY
In phone calls over the past two weeks, Trump asked for opinions from Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan, who both urged him not to resume attacks on Iran, according to a senior US official and another person familiar with the matter. They said Trump made no commitment either way.
Trump told bin Salman on 31 October that he was planning to attack after the elections, but the crown prince pleaded for him to hold off, arguing that economic sanctions against Iran were working, according to two more people familiar with the discussion.
Saudi Arabia's Foreign Ministry did not respond to a request for comment.
Trump has spoken with Erdogan three times since

data.title: Middle East Eye: Car bomb in Damascus suburb kills two, including child
data.author: Hilal Saki
data.summary:
Car bomb in Damascus suburb kills two, including child
A car bomb killed two people, including a child, and wounded another, in a suburb of Damascus on Saturday, Syrian Arab News Agency (Sana) said.
Authorities had "established a security perimeter at the scene and opened an investigation", it cited security forces as saying.
Syria has frequently been hit by explosions or attacks against civilians or security forces since the fall of former president Bashar al-Assad in December 2024.
In August another blast struck Jaramana, with the attack on a bus wounding 14 people, according to Sana.
In the capital Damascus, two devices exploded near a hotel where French President Emmanuel Macron was staying during a landmark visit in July. That blast left one person dead and 36 wounded.
Authorities blamed an organisation affiliated with the Islamic State group, which has previously claimed several attacks targeting Syrian security forces.
Report by AFP

data.title: Middle East Eye: WSJ: Iran still has 1,500-2,500 missiles, influencing US plans for renewed war
data.author: Hilal Saki
data.summary:
WSJ: Iran still has 1,500-2,500 missiles, influencing US plans for renewed war
American intelligence believes that Iran has some 1,500-2,500 missiles, and the apparent size of the arsenal has impacted Trump administration's decision on whether to resume strikes on the Islamic Republic, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing officials.
The officials told the newspaper that it is a “low confidence assessment” given the difficulties in tracking Tehran’s munitions, but that it was clear that the regime still possessed a large number of missiles.
The report says Israeli officials believe Tehran has over 1,500 ballistic missiles.
On Friday, Deputy Commander of the Islamic Revolution Guards Corps Major General Mostafa Izadi, said Iranian forces were capable of launching missiles equipped with two-ton warheads at targets 1,500 kilometres away.
Last Saturday, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it has lifted its self-imposed 2,000km limit on the range of its ballistic missiles.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Iraq sacks nine officials over oil smuggling in pro-Iran group's bastion
data.author: Hilal Saki
data.summary:
Iraq sacks nine officials over oil smuggling in pro-Iran group's bastion
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi dismissed nine officials on Saturday, following an investigation into allegations of oil smuggling in the Jurf al-Sakher area, a stronghold of the Iran-backed Kataeb Hezbollah group.
"In light of the investigation's findings," Zaidi "ordered that all individuals accused of involvement in oil smuggling operations be referred to the judiciary," his military spokesman Sabah al-Numan said, without identifying the suspects.
The premier "also ordered the dismissal" of nine officials, including security and intelligence officers in Babylon province, an interior ministry commander, and the director of the Oil Pipelines Company at the oil ministry.
Numan did not elaborate on the role of the sacked officials in the alleged smuggling operations.
A committee investigating the allegations entered Jurf al-Sakher on Friday, accompanied by members of Kataeb Hezbollah.
On Wednesday, the state news agency INA reported that "intelligence documents" containing satellite images "showed crude oil and oil-derivatives smuggling operations carried out by an armed faction" in Jurf al-Sakher, accusing the unnamed faction of tapping into a pipeline there.
According to Numan, the investigating committee "confirmed the accuracy" of the information.
Report by AFP

data.title: Middle East Eye: ‘Looking away was never a choice for me’: How Hollywood’s love affair with Israel turned sour
data.author: Fleur Hargreaves
data.summary:
‘Looking away was never a choice for me’: How Hollywood’s love affair with Israel turned sour
Submitted by
Fleur Hargreaves
on
Mon, 11/02/2026 - 10:59
A growing number of actors and film workers have been challenging their industry’s ‘deep complicity’ with Israel to end the toxic relationship
US actress Hannah Einbinder wears an 'Artists4Ceasefire' pin as she attends the 83rd annual Golden Globe Awards at the Beverly Hilton hotel in Beverly Hills, California, on 11 January 2026 (Frederic J Brown/AFP)
Off
Once Israel could rely on Hollywood to have its reputation laundered, performing the role of a benign ally which shared the values and interests of the West.
However, a growing number of actors and prominent figures in film and TV are confronting the industry’s ongoing complicity with Israel's occupation and its actions in Gaza, which a consensus of experts and human rights groups have called a genocide.
More and more artists are using their platforms to speak about the plight of the Palestinians and have contributed to Israel’s cratering approval among western audiences.
In 2025, US-based organisation Film Workers for Palestine (FWP), established by a group of filmmakers the previous year, released a pledge to end complicity with the genocide in Gaza.
It garnered the signatures of more than 5,500 people in the industry, including A-list actors like Josh O’Connor, Olivia Colman, Andrew Garfield, Emma Stone and many more.
Inspired by Filmmakers United Against Apartheid, a group of artists who refused to screen their work in apartheid South Africa, signatories pledged not to screen films, appear at or work alongside Israeli film institutions implicated in genocide and apartheid.
“People were ready to publicly put their name to a commitment of refusal... to not be complicit in Israel’s genocide,” an FWP spokesperson told Middle East Eye, adding that there is “power in numbers”.

Iran blames Israel for cyber attack on supermarket fridges
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has warned France against falling into an Israeli “false flag” trap after Paris accused an Iranian cyber unit of attacking refrigeration systems at hundreds of supermarkets.
IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebbi dismissed the French allegations as “ridiculous”, accusing Israel of seeking to turn European countries against Tehran and secure their support.
“Paris should beware of the Zionist regime's false flag trap,” Mohebbi wrote on X on Saturday.

“Paris should beware of the Zionist regime's false flag trap,” Mohebbi wrote on X on Saturday.
He also said that, unlike the United States and Israel, the IRGC did not target civilians.
France accused Shahid Kaveh, an offensive cyber unit within the IRGC’s Electronic Warfare and Cyber Defence Organisation, of carrying out the cyber attacks.
The attacks targeted refrigeration control systems at over 700 retail outlets on the night of 11-12 October, causing fires, serious damage and losses of food worth tens of millions of euros, the French foreign ministry said.
Paris said it would summon Iran's ambassador and propose new sanctions against individuals and entities within the European Union.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Jordan condemns Iranian drone strike on Bahrain
data.author: Areeb Ullah
data.summary:
Jordan condemns Iranian drone strike on Bahrain
Jordan joined other regional partners in condemning Iran’s targeting of Bahrain amid uncertainty over whether the war involving Iran, the United States and Israel would continue.
A Jordanian foreign ministry spokesperson described the attacks as a “dangerous escalation and a blatant breach of international law”.
The spokesperson condemned “Iran’s brutal attacks on the sister kingdom of Bahrain” as a violation of its sovereignty and a threat to its security, stability and territorial integrity.

data.title: Middle East Eye: IRGC says Bahrain drone strike responded to ‘US aggression’ in southern Iran
data.author: Areeb Ullah
data.summary:
IRGC says Bahrain drone strike responded to ‘US aggression’ in southern Iran
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it had launched a drone strike on a US airbase in Bahrain in response to an American attack on a telecommunications tower in southern Iran.
Speaking to Sepah News, an IRGC spokesperson said the force had used “six drones” to target “the radar of the US defence site at the al-Riffa helicopter base in Bahrain”.
“Expensive American drones are being shot down one after another, and a greater number of IRGC drones are heading towards American targets at this stage than in the previous stage, so the enemy knows any aggression will result in a tough and calculated response,” the spokesperson said.
